paragraphs.title: Rebuke for Unfaithfulness and Proof of God’s Knowledge

easy.explanation: The passage begins, “Hear ye this, O house of Jacob.”
easy.q: To whom does the prophet speak at the beginning of the passage?

easy.explanation: The people are described as those “which swear by the name of the Lord.”
easy.q: By whose name did the people swear?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “thy neck is an iron sinew.”
easy.q: How is the people’s neck described?

answers: So the people would not say that their idols had done them
So they could build a new city
So they would leave for Egypt
medium.explanation: The Lord showed events beforehand lest the people should say, “Mine idol hath done them.”
medium.q: Why did the Lord declare events beforehand?

answers: Hidden things that they did not know
medium.explanation: The Lord says He showed them “new things” and “hidden things,” which they did not know.
medium.q: How are the new things described that the Lord revealed?

medium.explanation: The word describes the people’s stubborn refusal to respond faithfully to God.
medium.q: What does “obstinate” mean in this passage?

answers: They are called by the name of Israel, but they do not act in truth or righteousness
They live in a city, but they travel in the wilderness
They hear, but they cannot speak
challenge.explanation: They are called by the name of Israel, yet the passage says they are “not in truth, nor in righteousness.”
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in the description of the people?

answers: That the Lord knew them beforehand and brought them to pass
That the people invented the events
challenge.explanation: The Lord declared the events before they occurred and then performed them.
challenge.q: What does the Lord’s announcing events before they happened demonstrate?

answers: To show that they were a new revelation from the Lord
To prove that the people were already prophets
To explain why they left Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The repeated statements emphasize that these matters were newly revealed by God.
challenge.q: Why does the passage emphasize that the people did not hear or know the new things?

paragraphs.title: Patience, Refinement, and the Preservation of God’s Honor

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “For my name’s sake will I defer mine anger.”
easy.q: For whose sake does the Lord defer His anger?

answers: As refinement in the furnace of affliction
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction.”
easy.q: How is the people’s refining described?

easy.explanation: He says, “I am the first, I also am the last.”
easy.q: How does the Lord describe Himself in relation to time?

answers: To preserve the honor of His name
Because the people had never sinned
medium.explanation: The Lord acts for His name’s sake and will not allow His name to be polluted.
medium.q: Why does the Lord refrain from cutting off the people?

medium.explanation: The Lord’s hand founded the earth and His right hand spanned the heavens.
medium.q: What do the descriptions of the Lord founding the earth and spanning the heavens emphasize?

medium.explanation: The image of a furnace presents suffering as a process of testing and purification.
medium.q: What does “refined” mean in the context of this passage?

answers: The Lord does not destroy them immediately but leads them through suffering and refinement
The Lord removes every expectation from them
The Lord replaces them with another nation
challenge.explanation: Instead of cutting them off, the Lord defers His anger and refines them in affliction.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the Lord’s patience and the people’s refinement?

answers: That the Lord acts to preserve the honor of His name
That the Lord acts only for Babylon
That the Lord acts without a purpose
challenge.explanation: The repeated phrase strongly emphasizes the Lord’s concern for His own name and glory.
challenge.q: What does the repetition in “For mine own sake, even for mine own sake” emphasize?

answers: That the message comes with divine authority and a commission
That the prophet has withdrawn his message
challenge.explanation: The passage ends with the Lord God and His Spirit sending the speaker.
challenge.q: What does the passage’s movement from addressing Jacob to speaking of the one who was sent suggest?

paragraphs.title: God’s Guidance and the Blessing of Obedience

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I am the Lord thy God which teacheth thee to profit.”
The Lord says, “then had thy peace been as a river.”
easy.q: What would Israel’s peace have been like if they had listened?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Thy seed also had been as the sand.”
easy.q: What would Israel’s seed have been like?

medium.explanation: The blessings are introduced by the words, “O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments!”
medium.q: What was the condition for receiving the blessings described?

medium.explanation: The passage mentions peace like a river, righteousness like the waves of the sea, and abundant seed.
medium.q: What results would have followed obedience?

medium.explanation: The Lord teaches His people in the way that is beneficial for them.
medium.q: What does “to profit” mean in verse 17?

challenge.explanation: A river and the waves of the sea suggest an abundant and continual supply.
challenge.q: What do the images of peace as a river and righteousness as waves of the sea communicate?

answers: The Lord provides a beneficial way, but Israel does not listen
The Lord gives Israel no guidance
Israel teaches the Lord the way
challenge.explanation: The Lord teaches and leads them, but the passage presents obedience as an unfulfilled condition.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the Lord’s guidance and Israel’s disobedience?

answers: The continuing existence of Israel’s descendants
The immediate abandonment of the land
challenge.explanation: The statement describes the preservation and continuation of Israel’s offspring.
challenge.q: What does the promise that Israel’s name would not be cut off or destroyed emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Departure from Babylon and the Proclamation of Redemption

easy.explanation: The command is, “Go ye forth of Babylon, flee ye from the Chaldeans.”
easy.q: From which city were the people commanded to depart?

answers: That the Lord had redeemed His servant Jacob
That they had found houses in the wilderness
easy.explanation: They were to declare, “The Lord hath redeemed his servant Jacob.”
easy.q: What were the people to proclaim with a voice of singing?

easy.explanation: The Lord caused waters to flow out of the rock for them.
easy.q: What did the Lord provide in the wilderness?

answers: With singing and to the end of the earth
medium.explanation: They were to declare it with a voice of singing and utter it “even to the end of the earth.”
medium.q: How were the people to proclaim their redemption?

answers: It recalls the Lord’s care and guidance of His people
It proves that Babylon was a watery city
It explains why the people should remain in Babylon
medium.explanation: The miracle shows that the Lord can provide for His people during their journey.
medium.q: What does the memory of water from the rock contribute to the passage?

medium.explanation: The chapter ends, “There is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked.”
medium.q: What is said about the wicked at the end of the chapter?

answers: The departure is both an action and a joyful message to be spread
The proclamation removes the need to leave
challenge.explanation: The people are commanded both to leave Babylon and to announce the Lord’s redemption publicly.
challenge.q: What connection is made between leaving Babylon and proclaiming redemption?

answers: The Lord can provide for His people even in difficult conditions
The people never needed the Lord’s help
The wilderness was naturally full of water
challenge.explanation: Water from the rock demonstrates the Lord’s ability to sustain His people in the wilderness.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the repeated mention of water provided from the rock?

answers: Jacob receives a message of redemption, while the wicked have no peace
Jacob has no hope, while the wicked have peace
Both Jacob and the wicked are described as having peace
challenge.explanation: The passage joins a joyful proclamation of redemption with the warning that the wicked have no peace.
challenge.q: What contrast is created between Jacob’s redemption and the chapter’s final statement?
